chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Global Central Banks India Watches

lessons.title: ECB, BoJ, and PBoC: The Other Central Banks That Matter

body.text: The Fed is not the only central bank that can move Dalal Street. The European Central Bank sets money for India's biggest new trade partner bloc, the Bank of Japan controls the world's cheapest source of borrowed money, and the People's Bank of China steers the economy India buys the most from. When any of them shifts course, global money gets rerouted, and India is often on the receiving end.

children.text: In the last two lessons you saw how the Fed's rates and balance sheet reach India. This lesson introduces the three other central banks that matter most for Indian markets, explains how each one affects India, and walks through two real episodes where decisions in Tokyo and Beijing caused sharp moves in the Nifty.
The Big Three at a Glance

body.title: Major Central Bank Policy Rates, Mid-September 2026 (%)

body.text: Notice how India's rate sits above all four. That extra yield is part of what attracts foreign money to Indian bonds. But when the ECB, the BoJ and possibly the Fed are all raising rates at once, as in 2026, India's advantage shrinks, which is one reason foreign investors have been pulling money out.

children.text: The European Central Bank

The ECB sets monetary policy for the 21 countries that use the euro, after Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026. It became famous during the 2012 euro crisis, when President Mario Draghi pledged to do whatever it takes to save the currency, and it later ran its own large QE programme and even pushed rates below zero.
The 2026 Turn

After cutting its deposit rate to 2% in 2025, the ECB reversed course when the Iran war pushed energy prices up. It raised rates for the first time in about three years in June 2026, to 2.25%, and again on 10 September 2026, to 2.50%, with euro area inflation at 3.3% and energy inflation at 14.3% in August. Lagarde called the September hike a no-brainer, but declined to signal what comes next.

cells: India and the EU concluded negotiations on a landmark free trade agreement on 27 January 2026. Weaker euro area demand from higher rates can hurt Indian exporters of textiles, engineering goods, chemicals and IT services.
European pension funds and asset managers are major foreign investors in Indian stocks and bonds. Higher euro yields make home markets more attractive.
ECB hikes can strengthen the euro against the dollar, which tends to weaken the dollar index and can ease pressure on the rupee.

children.text: The Bank of Japan and the Carry Trade

markDefs.definition: Borrowing in Japanese yen at very low interest rates and investing the money in higher-yielding assets elsewhere, such as US or Indian bonds and stocks, to profit from the rate gap.

children.text: For most of the past three decades, Japan had near-zero or negative interest rates. That made the yen the world's cheapest currency to borrow, and investors used it to fund the
yen carry trade
: borrow cheaply in yen, convert the money, and invest it in higher-yielding assets abroad, including US tech stocks and emerging markets like India.
A hedge fund borrows yen at close to zero interest.
It converts the yen into dollars or rupees.
It buys higher-yielding assets: US stocks, Indian bonds, Indian stocks.
It profits from the rate gap, as long as the yen does not strengthen sharply.
If the yen jumps, the loan becomes more expensive to repay, and the fund rushes to sell its foreign assets and buy back yen.

body.title: When the Carry Trade Goes Wrong
body.prompt: An investor borrows yen at 0.5% a year and invests in Indian government bonds yielding 7.0%. Over the year, the yen strengthens 8% against the rupee, so repaying the yen loan costs 8% more in rupee terms. Ignoring other costs, what is the investor's approximate return, in percent? Enter a negative number for a loss.
body.explanation: Return ≈ bond yield − borrowing cost − currency loss = 7.0% − 0.5% − 8.0% = -1.5%. A trade that looked like an easy 6.5% becomes a loss. When thousands of investors face this at once, they all sell their foreign assets together, which is exactly what happened in August 2024.

children.text: Case: The Yen Shock of August 2024

body.title: How a Small BoJ Hike Shook the World

events.title: BoJ ends negative rates
events.description: After eight years below zero, the BoJ exits negative interest rates and yield curve control.

events.title: Surprise hike to 0.25%
events.description: A small move by global standards, but a signal that cheap yen borrowing was ending.

events.title: Weak US jobs data
events.description: US employers add only 114,000 jobs in July, far below forecasts, raising bets on Fed cuts and narrowing the US-Japan rate gap further.

events.title: The carry trade unwinds
events.description: The yen surges as investors rush to repay yen loans. Japan's Nikkei plunges 12.4%, its worst day since 1987. In India, the Sensex falls 2,222.55 points, or 2.74%, to 78,759.40, and the Nifty 50 drops 2.68% to 24,055.60.

body.text: The BoJ move itself was only 15 basis points, from around 0.1% to 0.25%. Its impact came from how much money around the world had been borrowed in yen. Small changes at a central bank that funds global leverage can have outsized effects, far from home.

children.text: Japan in 2026

The BoJ kept normalising. It raised rates to 0.50% in January 2025, 0.75% in December 2025 and 1.00% in June 2026, the highest since 1995. At its July 2026 meeting it held at 1.00% by an 8 to 1 vote, with one member wanting a hike to 1.25%, and Governor Ueda flagged upside risks to inflation. Its next decision was due on 17 and 18 September 2026. Each step higher makes the yen carry trade less attractive and is a risk to watch for global markets.

body.title: Why Did India Fall on 5 August 2024?
body.question: The Bank of Japan raised rates by just 15 basis points in July 2024, yet the Nifty fell 2.68% on 5 August. What best explains the link?
options: Japan is India's largest export market
Investors who had borrowed cheap yen to buy global assets rushed to sell those assets, including Indian stocks, when the yen surged
The BoJ directly controls Indian interest rates
Indian companies had borrowed heavily from the BoJ
body.explanation: The yen carry trade linked Japanese interest rates to markets everywhere. When the yen strengthened sharply, leveraged investors had to sell foreign assets to repay yen loans. That forced selling hit US tech stocks, Asian markets and India alike, and FPIs sold over ₹10,000 crore of Indian shares that day.

children.text: The People's Bank of China

The PBoC works differently from the RBI or the Fed. It is not independent in the Western sense: it operates under the direction of China's State Council. It uses a mix of tools, including its 7-day reverse repo rate, the Loan Prime Rate that banks use to price loans, and the reserve requirement ratio, which works like India's CRR. The 7-day rate has been 1.40% since May 2025, and the one-year and five-year Loan Prime Rates have stayed at 3.0% and 3.5%.

stats.label: India-China trade, FY26
stats.context: China became India's largest trading partner

body.title: How Lopsided Is the Trade?
body.prompt: In FY26, India's total trade with China was $151.1 billion, of which imports from China were $131.63 billion. What share of the total trade were imports, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: $131.63 billion ÷ $151.1 billion × 100 = 87.1%. That leaves exports to China of only about $19.5 billion. Because India buys so much from China, especially electronics, machinery, chemicals and battery components, PBoC decisions that move China's economy and the yuan quickly affect Indian input costs and manufacturers.

children.text: Case: "Sell India, Buy China", October 2024

On 24 September 2024, PBoC Governor Pan Gongsheng unveiled China's biggest stimulus package since the pandemic: a 50 basis point cut in the reserve requirement ratio to 9.5%, a cut in the 7-day reverse repo rate from 1.7% to 1.5%, lower mortgage rates, smaller down payments for second homes, and a new swap facility to help institutions buy stocks. Chinese stocks rallied hard.

Global fund managers, who had seen Indian valuations as expensive, moved money from India to China. In October 2024, FPIs pulled a record net ₹94,017 crore out of Indian equities in a single month, with financials among the hardest hit. It was a clear lesson that India competes with China for global investment money, and a PBoC decision can redirect those flows almost overnight.

body.title: Go Deeper: When All the Big Central Banks Move Together

children.text: In 2026, the ECB and the BoJ were both hiking, and the Fed looked set to follow. When the world's major central banks tighten at the same time, the effects stack up: global liquidity shrinks, borrowing costs rise everywhere and money becomes more selective about where it goes.

For India, that meant record foreign equity outflows, a weaker rupee and pressure on the RBI to tighten despite slowing growth. The PBoC stood apart, leaning towards easing, which kept China in the running as a destination for global funds. Watching all four central banks together gives a far clearer picture than watching the Fed alone.

body.title: Three Headlines in One Week
body.scenario: Imagine one week in late 2026 brings three headlines: the BoJ hikes to 1.25% and hints at more; the ECB signals a pause after its September hike; and the PBoC announces a large rate cut and property stimulus. You manage a portfolio of Indian large-cap stocks.
body.prompt: How might each headline affect Indian markets, and which one worries you most?
body.modelAnswer: The BoJ hike is the biggest short-term risk. Higher Japanese rates and a stronger yen can trigger another unwinding of yen carry trades, forcing leveraged investors to sell global assets, including Indian stocks, as happened in August 2024. The ECB pause is mildly positive: it eases pressure on global yields and European investors' preference for home markets, and could weaken the euro, which tends to lift the dollar slightly. The PBoC stimulus is a two-sided story. It could pull global fund money from India to China, as in October 2024, especially if Indian valuations look stretched. But a stronger Chinese economy can also support demand for commodities and global growth, and cheaper Chinese inputs can help Indian manufacturers. In the near term, the BoJ headline and possible "sell India, buy China" flows are the main worries, so watch FPI flow data and the yen closely.

body.title: Build Your Global Central Bank Tracker
steps: Note the current policy rates of the RBI, the Fed, the ECB, the BoJ and the PBoC in one table
Look up the outcome of the BoJ's 17 and 18 September 2026 meeting and whether the yen moved sharply
Check the USD/JPY exchange rate once a week for signs of a sudden yen rally
Find the latest monthly FPI flow data from NSDL and see whether money is moving towards China or other markets
Follow the progress of the India-EU trade agreement and note which Indian sectors stand to gain

points: The ECB, the BoJ and the PBoC all move global money in ways that reach India, not just the US Fed.
The ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.25% in June and 2.50% in September 2026 as the Iran war lifted euro area inflation to 3.3%.
The BoJ has raised rates from below zero in early 2024 to 1.00% in June 2026; higher Japanese rates threaten the yen carry trade that funds global risk-taking.
On 5 August 2024, a yen carry trade unwind helped push the Nikkei down 12.4% and the Nifty down 2.68% in a single day.
The PBoC operates under China's State Council; its September 2024 stimulus helped trigger a record ₹94,017 crore FPI outflow from India in October 2024.
China is India's largest trading partner, with a record $112.16 billion trade deficit in FY26, so PBoC policy also affects Indian input costs.
